acceptedWorkstreams.title: Map every legacy URL from four sources, then ship one reviewed redirect table
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Old addresses are not discoverable by guessing, so collect them from four places and say where each came from: press pages that still link to the old name, the Internet Archive CDX for the Telex and zeduchat domains, hardcoded URLs inside the repository, and any social or directory profile that still uses an old link. Classify each into one of three outcomes only: 301 to the live page that serves the same intent, 410 if no page serves that intent, or leave alone if it already works. Then implement the table as one redirects file and add a check that every old path returns a single 301 to a destination that answers 200, with the destination fetched on the day of delivery. Work: 1) collect and dedupe with a source column; 2) decide the outcome per URL and flag the judgement calls for the team; 3) write the redirects file; 4) run the check and attach its output. Deliver: the table, the change, the check output, and a short list of URLs where the honest answer is 410 rather than a redirect.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Restore DNS for telex.im first, then a one-hop 301 map from real backlinks
acceptedWorkstreams.description:
Checked 22 Oct 2026: telex.im, www.telex.im and zeduchat.com do not resolve at all (curl: could not resolve host), so a redirect table in the Zedu app alone cannot fix them; every old link is dead before it reaches our server. Separately, unknown paths on zedu.chat return 200 (for example /telex), so old paths silently land on a soft page rather than a 404 or the right page.

Approach: 1) confirm with the team who controls the telex.im and zeduchat domains, and point them at an edge redirect (Cloudflare redirect rule or a tiny redirect host), since the app never sees those requests; 2) build the legacy URL list from real sources: the Wayback Machine CDX index for telex.im, press articles that cite Telex, and the current Telex social bios; 3) map each old path to the one current zedu.chat page with the same intent, with a 410 where nothing fits; 4) test every row with curl, one hop to a 200 page.

Limit: step 1 needs DNS or Cloudflare access from the team; without it the deliverable is the tested map plus the exact rule to paste in.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Set a retirement date for each old path instead of promising it will redirect forever
acceptedWorkstreams.description: A redirect table that nobody revisits grows into a permanent second URL structure, and every future page has to remember it. Give the old paths an end. Work: for each old path, record the traffic it still receives from the server logs or analytics over the last ninety days, then assign one of three outcomes with a date: redirect until a set month and then return 410, keep indefinitely because something printed still points at it, or remove now because nothing has requested it in the window. Deliver the table with the traffic figure behind each decision, the dates, and the one-line check that runs before the date arrives so a path with sudden traffic is not retired by accident.

Those are the ones we control completely and the ones a customer clicks months later. Work: search the repository and the email templates for every URL that points at the old name, list them with the file or template they live in, and fix them at the source rather than redirecting after the fact. Then give the redirect map the ones that have already left the building and cannot be edited. Deliver the inventory with file references, the fixes, and the residual list that only a redirect can save.

acceptedWorkstreams.description: A redirect map is a snapshot, and old links keep arriving from places no crawl reaches: a slide deck, a blog post, a partner page. After the map ships, keep watching. Work: collect the 404s and near-misses for old-looking paths from the server logs and the analytics for thirty days, review them once a week, and add a redirect or a 410 only where the traffic and the intent justify it. This is the part that turns a one-off map into something that holds.
